# Silicosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Restrictive lung diseases > Silicosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Oh0IVf)

---

## Summary

Silicosis is a common <u>occupational lung disease</u> that is caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica dust. Silica is the most abundant mineral on earth. Workers that are involved for example in constructions, mining, or glass production are among the individuals with the highest risk of developing the condition. Acute silicosis causes severe symptoms (e.g., <u>exertional dyspnea</u>, <u>cough</u> with <u>sputum</u>) and has a very poor prognosis. Chronic silicosis has a very variable prognosis and affected individuals may remain asymptomatic for several decades. However, radiographic signs are usually seen early on. Typical radiographic findings are calcifications of perihilar <u>lymph nodes</u>, diffuse <u>ground glass opacities</u>, large numbers of rounded, solitary <u>nodules</u> or bigger, confluent opacities. Avoiding further exposure to silica is crucial, especially since the only treatment available is symptomatic (e.g., <u>bronchodilators</u>). Silicosis is associated with an increased risk of <u>tuberculosis</u> and <u>lung cancer</u>.

---

## Etiology

* Inhalation of crystalline silica, most commonly as dust

* High-risk occupations for the development of silicosis include sandblasting, mining;  (e.g., coal mining), construction;  (e.g., tunnel construction), hydraulic fracturing, ceramics production, quarrying, glass manufacturing, and working in foundries.





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the high-risk occupations for the development of silicosis, think “I found (foundries) sand (sandblasting) on my (mining) window sill (silicosis)!”




References:[[2]](/library/ewax35)[[4]](/library/bxbHED)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Inhalation of silica dust → deposition in the <u>airways</u>;   → interaction of crystalline silica surfaces with aqueous media produces oxygen radicals → inflammatory reaction and injury to pulmonary cells (e.g., <u>alveolar macrophages</u>);   → <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u> and scarring




References:[[4]](/library/bxbHED)[[5]](/library/p30Ljf)

---

## Clinical features

### Acute silicosis




Acute silicosis refers to a short-term exposure to a large amount of crystalline silica dust.




* Within days to weeks

* <u>Dyspnea</u>, <u>cough</u>

* Pleuritic <u>pain</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* Within months to years

* Weight loss

* Fatigue

* <u>Cyanosis</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u>





### Chronic silicosis




Chronic silicosis refers to long-term exposure to crystalline silica dust. Patients may remain completely asymptomatic or develop symptoms only after several decades of exposure.




* <u>Chronic cough</u>;  (often with <u>sputum</u>; ) and <u>exertional dyspnea</u>

* Fatigue and weight loss

* <u>Signs of respiratory failure</u> and <u>cor pulmonale</u>

* Caplan syndrome: <u>pneumoconiosis</u> in combination with <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>; characterized by rapid development of basilar <u>nodules</u> and mild obstruction of ventilation [[6]](/library/dxbovD)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Dyspnea</u> upon exertion and <u>cough</u> with <u>sputum</u> are the key clinical features of silicosis!




> [!NOTE]
> Symptoms of chronic silicosis are variable and often occur only after several decades after constant/repeated exposure!References: [[4]](/library/bxbHED)[[7]](/library/WxbPvD)

---

## Diagnosis

Silicosis is diagnosed based on the occupational history, respiratory symptoms, and the following diagnostic investigations. See also “<u>Overview of pneumoconioses</u>”.




* <u>Chest x-ray</u> 

* Eggshell calcification: well-defined sickle-shaped calcification of the rims of <u>hilar lymph nodes</u>

* Bilateral diffuse <u>ground glass opacities</u>

* Large number of rounded, solitary, small (≤ 1 cm in diameter) opacities particularly in the upper lobe of the <u>lungs</u>

* Confluence of solitary lesions to form opacities that gradually enlarge to ≥ 1 cm

* <u>Lung function tests</u>: ↓ <u>FVC</u>, ↓ TLC, ↓ <u>FEV1</u>, ↓ <u>FEV1/FVC ratio</u> → findings indicate a mix of restrictive and <u>obstructive lung disease</u>

* <u>Pulse oximetry</u>/<u>ABG</u>: reduced <u>oxygen saturation</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u>: silicotic nodules, characterized by weakly <u>birefringent</u> silica particles in a central <u>hyalinized</u> region surrounded by concentric "onion-<u>skin</u>" <u>collagen fibers</u>

> [!NOTE]
> In the early stages of the disease, there may not be any symptoms or findings on <u>auscultation</u> (<u>wheezing</u> or buzzing), while radiographic abnormalities can already be seen!




> [!NOTE]
> Silicosis features pathologic changes of both restrictive and <u>obstructive lung disease</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Silica is found below the earth's surface, but the upper lobes of the <u>lungs</u> are primarily affected.




References: [[4]](/library/bxbHED)[[7]](/library/WxbPvD)

---

## Treatment

* There is no definitive treatment for either acute or chronic silicosis.

* Avoid further exposure to crystalline silica

* <u>Lung transplantation</u> (in patients with advanced <u>respiratory failure</u>)

* Symptomatic treatment

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Bronchodilators</u>

* <u>Supplemental oxygen</u>

* <u>Vaccination</u> against pathogens causing respiratory infections (e.g., <u>pneumococci</u>)





References:[[3]](/library/fwakR5)[[4]](/library/bxbHED)[[7]](/library/WxbPvD)

---

## Complications

* <u>Tuberculosis</u> (silicotuberculosis)

* Advanced silicosis increases the risk of <u>tuberculosis</u>.

* Silica disrupts <u>macrophage</u> <u>phagolysosomes</u> → release of phagolysosomal contents → <u>apoptosis</u> of pulmonary <u>macrophages</u> → impaired pulmonary immune response → increased risk of <u>tuberculosis</u> [[8]](/library/uebp0G)

* Annual <u>TB skin testing</u> is recommended in patients with advanced silicosis

* <u>Lung cancer</u>: silicosis doubles the risk for developing <u>lung cancer</u>.

* See also “Chronic silicosis” in “Clinical features.”





References:[[5]](/library/p30Ljf)[[9]](/library/gwaFR5)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
